snippet.description:
In Los Angeles the rise of street gangs, the Bloods and the Crips, bring murder and drugs to the streets of South Central. In 1970s and 1980s, loosely affiliated African American street gangs were waging a 20-year turf war. Born of the revolutionary anti-racist ideology of the 60s, the 'gangstas' soon turn to a life crime. The emerging crack cocaine trade fuels staggering levels of bloodshed. snippet.title: How Forensic Science Exposes Murderers Who Stage Crime Scenes
snippet.description:
Step inside three shocking murder cases where killers staged crime scenes and only forensic science revealed the truth behind tainted blood and deception.

In this gripping true crime episode, forensic experts unravel the mysteries behind three seemingly straightforward deaths: a young woman struck by a train in Florida, a wife who vanishes without a trace in Arizona, and a brutal double homicide in California. Each case appears open and shut at first glance - suicide, missing person, self-defense - but beneath the surface, evidence tells a far darker story. Watch as investigators and forensic examiners use advanced bloodstain pattern analysis, DNA testing, and meticulous crime scene reconstruction to expose murderers who thought they could outsmart the system.

Discover how subtle clues like blood spatter, a broken hyoid bone, and staged wounds helped bring killers to justice, even when bodies were missing or crime scenes were carefully manipulated. If you’re fascinated by criminal psychology, forensic breakthroughs, or the relentless pursuit of justice, this video will keep you on the edge of your seat as it reveals how science catches murderers who try to cover their tracks.

Instead, it became one of the greatest military disasters in history. 🔔 Subscribe and join us on this journey around the world → https://bit.ly/WorldView-Documentary

July 1, 1916, 7:30am. In the Somme, 500,000 French and British soldiers, on a front stretching 40 km, launch the most senseless attack of an absurd war. Carrying 35 kg on their backs and with orders not to run or drop on the ground, they walk towards death as if on a parade. That morning, 60,000 men fall.

This absurd obstinate pursuit of an error would last 5 months.

With more than a million casualties on both sides, the Battle of the Somme would cost more lives than Verdun in twice as less time. For negligible results.

snippet.title: A Day in the Life of Al Capone
snippet.description:
It is October 18, 1928, and Al Capone is at the height of his power. From his bulletproof suite at the Lexington Hotel to the industrial breweries of Cicero, this video follows a single day in the life of America’s most famous criminal emperor.

Discover the corporate-style efficiency of the Chicago Outfit 📉. We look at how "Greasy Thumb" Guzik managed the ledgers and how Frank Nitti enforced the peace. Witness the paradox of a man who fed orphans 🥖 while running a shadow government built on "pineapples" and bribes 💣.

In this video, we explore:
-The architecture of paranoia: Suite 430 at the Lexington Hotel 🏨.
-The $30,000 armored 1928 Cadillac V-8 🚗.
-The "Pineapple Primary" and the corruption of Chicago politics 🗳️.
-The legendary generosity and terrifying brutality of the "Man on Navy Street."

snippet.title: Christchurch: From Earthquake Ruins to a Vibrant City Reborn
snippet.description:
Step into the heart of Christchurch, New Zealand’s Garden City, where ancient forests, vibrant street art, and powerful stories of resilience come alive. Discover how this city thrives after disaster.

In this immersive journey, we explore Christchurch’s rich history, from the tranquility of Riccarton Bush’s 600-year-old trees to the bustling pop-up malls that symbolize the city’s rebirth. Wander through Hadley Park’s green spaces, visit the childhood home of war hero Charles Upham, and relive the drama of the 2011 earthquake that reshaped the city’s skyline. You’ll ride on historic electric vans, marvel at the innovative Cardboard Cathedral, and witness how creative street art brings hope and color to the recovering urban landscape.

We dive deep into the legacy of women’s suffrage, celebrating Christchurch’s role in making New Zealand the first country to grant women the vote. Along the way, you’ll meet passionate locals, uncover archaeological treasures beneath old theaters, and see how a community’s determination fuels both recovery and reinvention. Whether you’re fascinated by history, inspired by resilience, or simply curious about the unique blend of old and new in Christchurch, this video offers a moving portrait of a city that refuses to be defined by tragedy.

snippet.description:
What happens when the man who built the world’s most powerful weapon turns against the system that created it? 🔔 Subscribe and join us on this journey around the world → https://bit.ly/WorldView-Documentary

00:00 Introduction

The most honored physicist of the Soviet regime was also its most inflexible dissident. Through his life, Iosif Pasternak offers a universal reflection on Russian history, humanism, and democratic values. Before the Soviet Parliament, the frail old man sometimes stumbled over his words, but his pronouncements resonated with extraordinary force. Whether denouncing the corruption of the elites or the Red Army's intervention in Afghanistan, the suffering of young recruits or the necessity of abolishing the single-party system, his simple sentences cut through the humdrum of empty rhetoric. The recording dates from 1989, and Mikhail Gorbachev, General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, is growing impatient at the podium, above the troublesome academician whom he has just released. Andrei Sakharov had returned only a few months earlier from Gorky, where he and his wife had been under house arrest in total isolation. He died shortly after this tumultuous session, and a huge crowd came to pay their respects to his body. In two decades, the physicist, adored for having developed the hydrogen bomb in 1953 before choosing to become a dissident, had become one of the most popular champions of democracy in Russia.

snippet.title: The Real 'Lefty Rosenthal' Was the Most Dangerous Man Behind Casino Movie
snippet.description:
October 4, 1982. A bomb explodes under Frank "Lefty" Rosenthal's Cadillac outside Tony Roma's in Las Vegas. He walks away. The movie Casino ends there. The real story doesn't. Because what Lefty Rosenthal did next is the version Hollywood never had the guts to film.

In this deep-dive documentary, we expose the true ending of the Ace Rothstein story. The one Martin Scorsese left on the cutting room floor. The skim. The marriage. The betrayal. The witness protection deal. And the 26 years of quiet retirement in Miami Beach that the Chicago Outfit could never avenge.

What you'll learn in this episode:
- How a steel stabilizer plate under a 1981 Cadillac Eldorado accidentally saved Lefty's life
- The exact mechanics of the $30 to $50 million Stardust skim operation
- Why Lefty was a Top Echelon FBI informant from 1961 under the codename "Achilles"
- The Geri McGee and Tony Spilotro affair that broke the friendship and triggered the hit
- How Lefty's testimony helped indict 15 Mafia bosses in the 1986 Strawman case
- The brutal cornfield murder of Tony and Michael Spilotro on June 14, 1986
- How Lefty died a free man in 2008, age 79, of natural causes in Miami Beach

Key figures: 
Frank "Lefty" Rosenthal, Geri McGee, Tony Spilotro, Joseph Aiuppa, Jackie Cerone, Frank Balistrieri. Locations: Stardust Casino, Tony Roma's East Sahara, Bensenville Illinois, Enos Indiana cornfield, Miami Beach.

Timeline: 
1929 birth in Chicago, 1961 bribery conviction and FBI flip, 1968 arrival in Vegas, 1976 gaming license denied, 1982 car bombing, 1986 Strawman convictions and Spilotro murders, 2008 death.

Why this story matters today: 
Casino (1995) remains one of the most watched mob films ever made, but it sold viewers a Hollywood ending that erased the most uncomfortable truth in American organized crime history. The smartest wiseguy in the room wasn't a wiseguy at all. He was an informant who outplayed both the FBI and the Mafia and died rich.

snippet.title: How US Marine Special Operations Actually Work | Authorized Account | Insider
snippet.description:
Nick Jones is a former US Marine Raider who served in MARSOC, the Marine Corps’ elite special operations unit.

After starting his career as an infantry mortarman and scout sniper, Jones went on to complete the rigorous Marine Raider training and deployed multiple times to Iraq and Jordan. In 2020, Jones was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during a chaotic firefight with ISIS fighters in northern Iraq in which he repeatedly charged into enemy fire to rescue wounded teammates despite being shot in the leg himself.

Jones speaks with Business Insider about Marine Raider selection, advanced infantry tactics, and operating alongside allied forces. He goes into detail about the intense realities of close-quarters combat and the firefight that led to his Navy Cross. Jones also reveals the mental and physical toll of combat, detailing his personal struggles with trauma, injury recovery, and alcoholism.

Following his retirement from active service, Jones has dedicated his career to supporting the veteran community. He is the founder of the Talons Reach Foundation, a nonprofit based in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

snippet.description:
Step into the dramatic skies of WWII as American bombers launch daring raids from the windswept Aleutian island of Adak, battling storms and enemy fire for Pacific supremacy.

Discover the untold story of the Aleutian Islands campaign, where U.S. forces braved relentless weather and fierce Japanese resistance to defend the Pacific Coast during World War II. This video explores the pivotal role of Adak Island - a remote, treeless outpost closer to Japan than any other American base - and how its strategic airfield and harbor became lifelines for bold bombing missions against enemy-held Kiska. snippet.description:
Kevin Weeks wasn’t just a soldier. He was Whitey Bulger’s shadow. The man who collected the cash, drove the car, guarded the door, and helped bury at least 3 victims in the basement of an unassuming South Boston triple-decker. He saw Bucky Barrett bled dry for over $1 million. 

He watched John McIntyre strangled with a rope when the gun jammed. He helped dig the grave for Deborah Hussey, killed by her own stepfather’s partner. And then, on Halloween night 1985, he helped move all 3 bodies to a wooded gully near the Neponset River, where they would lie undisturbed for nearly 15 years.

In this episode, you’ll discover:
- How Whitey recruited Weeks at Triple O’s Lounge in 1979
- The 5-step “rent” system that earned the Winter Hill Gang over $120,000 a week
- The FBI corruption that protected Bulger for 20 years
- The 1999 indictment that broke Weeks’s silence
- How Weeks led federal agents to 3 buried corpses in January 2000
- The chilling testimony that helped convict Whitey in 2013
- Why Weeks called his boss a “stone-cold killer who could talk about gardening one minute and strangle a woman the next”

Key figures: 
Kevin Weeks, James “Whitey” Bulger, Steve “The Rifleman” Flemmi, FBI agent John Connolly, federal prosecutor Fred Wyshak. 

Timeline: 1956 to 2018.

This story matters because it’s the moment the FBI’s most shameful chapter was exposed by the unlikeliest whistleblower in American crime history. A man who had buried the bodies dug them up to bury the system that let it happen.

Billy Queen was an undercover agent for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. He spent almost three years embedded in the Mongols Motorcycle club.

Queen speaks to Business Insider about the internal workings of the Mongols, how he rose to become an officer in the club, its hierarchy, its rules, and its war with the Hells Angels. In 2000, his infiltration led to the arrest and conviction of 53 members.

Queen also covers his upbringing as the son of an ATF agent and his military service in Vietnam with the 82nd Airborne Division and Special Forces, which he completed before joining the ATF. He describes the training and skills required for undercover work, emphasizing that it is an innate talent more than a learned skill.

Queen is the author of "Under and Alone: Infiltrating the World’s Most Violent Motorcycle Gang" and "Armed and Dangerous: The Hunt for One of America’s Most Wanted Criminals."

snippet.title: The Real Kray Twins: Britain’s Deadliest Gangster Brothers
snippet.description:
Real Events: 
London, 1966. A man walks into a Whitechapel pub, shoots another man in the head in front of a dozen witnesses, and walks out untouched. For 3 years, nobody talks. That was the power of Ronnie and Reggie Kray, the twin brothers who turned the East End into a private kingdom of fear, fashion, and systematic violence. 

Hollywood gave you Legend (2015) with Tom Hardy in slick suits and stylized brutality. We’re giving you the documented truth that the film softened, skipped, or completely rewrote.

In this in-depth investigation, you’ll learn:
- How the Krays built their protection racket from a £100 snooker hall into a £2,000-a-week empire
- The real story of George Cornell’s execution at The Blind Beggar on March 9, 1966
- Why witnesses stayed silent for 3 years while Scotland Yard burned through case after case
- The brutal truth about the Jack “The Hat” McVitie murder on October 29, 1967
- How Ronnie’s untreated paranoid schizophrenia drove the firm’s worst decisions
- What really happened to Reggie’s wife Frances Shea
- How Detective Nipper Read finally cracked the silence and made the arrests of May 1968
- The longest murder trial in British history and the 30-year sentences that followed
- What Legend (2015) got right, what it softened, and what it left out entirely

Key figures: 
Ronnie Kray, Reggie Kray, Charlie Kray, George Cornell, Jack McVitie, Frances Shea, Detective Leonard “Nipper” Read, Lord Boothby, the Richardson Gang.

This isn’t a story about gangster glamour. It’s a story about what happens when two damaged boys from a Bethnal Green slum decide that fear is the only currency worth collecting. It’s about the gap between myth and record, between a David Bailey portrait and a body bag. And it matters today because we’re still selling the same lie, that organized crime can be beautiful, that violence in a good suit becomes art. The Krays prove otherwise.

Sources include: BBC News archives on Nipper Read (https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-52201667), The Guardian’s accuracy review of Legend (https://www.theguardian.com/film/2015/sep/08/behind-the-legend-how-accurate-is-tom-hardys-krays-drama), and court documents from the 1969 Old Bailey trial.

snippet.title: The Real 'Noodles' Was the Most Dangerous Gangster Behind 'Once Upon A Time in America' Movie
snippet.description:
October 1, 1980. A 78 year old man dies quietly in Manhattan, New York. No headlines. No procession. Just a body and a manuscript he wrote 30 years earlier in a Sing Sing prison cell. His name was Herschel Goldberg. 

The world would only ever know him by his pen name, Harry Grey. And the book he wrote, The Hoods, would become Sergio Leone's 13 year obsession and the basis for one of the greatest crime films ever made, Once Upon a Time in America.

But the real story behind that film is not what you saw on screen.
In this deep dive investigation, we trace the actual world of New York's Lower East Side during Prohibition, the immigrant tenements where 200,000 people per square mile fought, stole, and bootlegged their way out of poverty. You'll learn the true history of the Jewish gangsters who built the architecture of modern American organized crime, decades before The Godfather and the Five Families became household names.

What you will learn in this documentary:
- Who Herschel Goldberg really was and how he turned his crimes into Leone's masterpiece
- How Monk Eastman commanded an army of 1,200 street criminals on the Bowery
- The mechanics of Waxey Gordon's $2 million a year bootlegging empire
- How Meyer Lansky and Bugsy Siegel built the Bugs and Meyer Mob from a Cannon Street garage
- The full inside story of Lepke Buchalter, Murder Inc, and the only major mob boss executed in the electric chair
- Why Sergio Leone spent 13 years chasing this book and turned down The Godfather to make it

Key figures covered: 
Herschel "Harry Grey" Goldberg, Monk Eastman, Waxey Gordon, Arnold Rothstein, Meyer Lansky, Bugsy Siegel, Lucky Luciano, Lepke Buchalter, Abe Reles, Sergio Leone, Robert De Niro.

Timeline: 
1875 to 1989, from the birth of Monk Eastman to the death of Sergio Leone.

This story matters because the blueprint of modern organized crime, the Commission, the syndicates, the contract murder system, was not drawn by the Italians who inherited it. It was drawn by Jewish kids from Henry Street, Delancey Street, and Hester Street. Once Upon a Time in America is the only major American film that tells their story, and the man who wrote it lived it.

snippet.title: From Saddlers to the Blitz: A Century of Life in Liverpool | S1E3 | A House Through Time
snippet.description:
Historian David Olusoga follows the story of the house in Liverpool from 1891 to 1945, a turbulent fifty year period encompassing two World Wars and the Great Depression. He tracks the story of the Snewings, a large family of saddlers who live in the house for over four decades, and follows their business through challenging times – death in the family, cut-throat competition, the First World War and the age of the motorcar.

On the Snewings' death, the Great Depression takes hold and Liverpool's inner city housing begins to decline. David sees the house become a shabby lodging house rented out to low-income tenants. Amongst the multiple residents who share the house at the start of the Second World War he discovers Jack Greenall – a docker keeping a secret from his employers, who works in one of the city's most dangerous environments during the height of the Liverpool Blitz.

Finally, David uncovers the poignant story of Robert and Sarah Ann Duffy. Robert, son of a lowly cotton porter, is born in the slums; his wife Sarah Ann, has had an unhappy childhood with her abusive mother. But the two meet and marry, and carve out a successful career in the tailoring business, eventually transcending the tragic circumstances of their pasts.

Different lives within these walls

Each episode of this fascinating, presenter-led history series tells the unique personal stories of all the people who lived in one particular house, from the time it was built until today.

Through a combination of first-hand testimony, archive film and careful detective work, we'll find out who the different residents were over time, from the first people onwards. We'll explore what their lives were like while they lived there, and how the house changed over the years. Ultimately, by following the stories of individual residents and the times in which they lived, we'll provide a distinctive social history of the UK over time and of the place they called home.

snippet.title: The Real Jimmy Hoffa Was the Most Dangerous Man the Mafia Ever Erased
snippet.description:
On July 30, 1975, Jimmy Hoffa walked into the parking lot of the Machus Red Fox restaurant in Bloomfield Township, Michigan, climbed into a maroon Mercury Marquis, and vanished forever. Martin Scorsese’s The Irishman told you Frank Sheeran pulled the trigger. The FBI’s own Hoffex report tells a very different story.

In this deep dive, we expose what investigators have known for nearly 50 years but Hollywood ignored. The men who actually drove Hoffa to his death were a New Jersey crew working directly under Genovese capo Anthony Provenzano, sanctioned by Pennsylvania boss Russell Bufalino, executed in cooperation with the Detroit Partnership. We trace the forensic evidence, the witness placements, the phone records, and the lab results that destroyed Sheeran’s confession within months of its publication.

What you’ll learn in this episode:
- Why Hoffa’s federal lawsuit threatened to expose 20 years of mob pension fund corruption
- The three men named in the FBI Hoffex report as the actual killers
- The forensic evidence that contradicts Frank Sheeran’s deathbed confession
- The Beaverland Street house blood test results that collapsed the Irishman narrative
- The 4 most credible theories about where Hoffa’s body actually went
- Why Sally Bugs Briguglio was executed on Mulberry Street in 1978
- How Russell Bufalino delivered the verdict that ended Hoffa’s life

Key figures covered: 
Jimmy Hoffa, Frank Sheeran, Russell Bufalino, Anthony Tony Pro Provenzano, Salvatore Sally Bugs Briguglio, Thomas Andretta, Gabriel Briguglio, Tony Giacalone, Frank Fitzsimmons, and Phil Brother Moscato.

This story matters today because the Hoffa case represents the most successful organized crime cover-up of the 20th century. With every primary witness now dead, the truth is finally surfacing through declassified FBI files and decades of investigative work. The version The Irishman sold you was fiction. The real story is darker, smarter, and far more disturbing.

snippet.description:
He carried two cardboard boxes into a Boston courtroom in 1997 and torched the dirtiest chapter in FBI history. His name was Edward McDonald, and Hollywood loved him so much that Scorsese cast him in Goodfellas to play himself.

In this deep dive, we trace the fourteen year war between a Brooklyn born federal prosecutor and the Boston FBI field office that was protecting James Whitey Bulger as a Top Echelon Informant. McDonald saw it first. McDonald said it loudest. And McDonald was the man Mark Wahlberg watched on tape before stepping into the role of Sergeant Sean Dignam in The Departed.

What you’ll learn in this episode:
• How a Bay Ridge kid from Xaverian High School became the only federal prosecutor willing to call Whitey Bulger a murderer in 1982
• The full inside story of the World Jai Alai murders of Roger Wheeler, John Callahan, and Brian Halloran
• How John Connolly walked Brian Halloran’s cooperation file straight to Bulger and got him killed on the Boston waterfront
• The real reason Martin Scorsese cast McDonald in Goodfellas instead of a professional actor
• How Judge Mark Wolf’s 661 page ruling, citing McDonald 47 times, finally exposed the Bureau
• What happened to Connolly, Morris, Flemmi, and Bulger in the end

Key figures: 
Edward McDonald, James Whitey Bulger, John Connolly, John Morris, Stephen Flemmi, Roger Wheeler, John Callahan, Brian Halloran, Judge Mark Wolf, Martin Scorsese, Nicholas Pileggi.

1977 to 2018. From McDonald joining the Eastern District Strike Force to Bulger’s murder in USP Hazelton.

snippet.title: Britain’s Worst Defeat of WWI - Russia's Great Winter Victory
snippet.description:
🎥 Watch 300+ exclusive videos on ✔ youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on modern warfare the Great War and the Ottoman history during the World War I. Previously we covered the Rise of the Ottoman Empire from the humble beginnings as a small Turkic Beylik to the Fall of Constantinople 1453 covering all the major battles including (https://youtu.be/TDLmsiqhgns) and the reign of Mehmet II (https://youtu.be/TbqMBfxtOTI). After the Ottoman victory at Gallipoli and Bulgaria’s entry into the First World War, Istanbul shifted troops across a vast empire to meet the challenges of 1916. In the frozen Caucasus, General Nikolai Yudenich launches a meticulously prepared Russian offensive against the supposedly impregnable fortress of Erzurum. Winter marches, surprise attacks, and brutal fighting for mountain forts shatter the Ottoman Third Army and send it reeling westward. But while the Ottomans lose Erzurum, they strike back elsewhere. In the Sinai desert, Kress von Kressenstein’s forces raid British outposts near Katia, exposing the vulnerability of the Suez Canal. Farther east, the siege of Kut becomes a catastrophe for the British Empire. Relief columns repeatedly smash against Ottoman trenches at Sheikh Sa’ad, the Wadi, Hanna, Dujaila, and Sannaiyat—suffering appalling losses as General Charles Townshend’s starving garrison waits in vain. This episode follows the Russian advance through Persia, the fall of Kut after 147 days, and the strategic consequences of Britain’s twin failures at Gallipoli and Mesopotamia. It is a story of snowbound assaults, desert raids, and one of the most devastating surrenders of the Great War. Across three fronts, commanders gamble men, artillery, supply lines, and imperial prestige at terrible human cost.
